ch04.note: Hōka-sō (放下僧): itinerant entertainer-monks of medieval Japan, half-priest and half-mountebank, who juggled, tumbled, spun tops and performed sleight of hand at roadsides and festivals. The crowd on the riverbank has gathered to watch just such street performers.

A low mountain among the eastern hills of Kyoto, rising beyond the Kamo river. Its western slope is Daimonji-yama, later the site of the giant character dai (大, “great”) traced in bonfires above the city each August for the Bon festival of the dead. Kisaru points the crowd at its peak to sell them the phantom storm-cloud.

ch04.anchor: Gion was not yet a quarter of teahouses
ch04.note: Gion, the district below the Yasaka Shrine on the east bank of the Kamo, became in later centuries Kyoto’s most famous pleasure-and-teahouse quarter, the haunt of the geisha. Shiba’s aside reminds the reader that in 1591 none of that yet existed: the road ran through farmland and temple ground.

Katō Kiyomasa (1562–1611), one of Hideyoshi’s foremost generals, holder of the court title Governor of Higo (Higo-no-kami) and lord of a great fief in Kyushu. That an Iga man who had entered his open service was hunted down and killed by his own former comrades shows how the shadow-clans policed the ones who left them for a lord’s pay.

Maeda Gen’i (1539–1602), a former Buddhist priest who rose to become Hideyoshi’s governor of Kyoto—the office the text calls the magistracy of the capital. He policed the city, oversaw its temples and shrines, and ran the web of informers that watched for spies and men of doubtful business: the very service Gohei has now entered under a false name. Gen’i later sat among Hideyoshi’s Five Commissioners of state.
